highlights.text: The policy states plainly that inputs are used to train Browser Use's AI models, and it names no setting, email address, or other mechanism for declining. Nothing in the text distinguishes paid tiers from free ones on this point.

highlights.title: A perpetual, sublicensable licence over your content
highlights.text: The terms take a worldwide, royalty-free, transferable, sublicensable through multiple tiers, perpetual and irrevocable licence to copy, store, modify and otherwise use user content, extending beyond operating the service to developing other Browser Use offerings.

highlights.title: No retention period and no breach notice
highlights.text: Data is kept "for as long as necessary" with no number attached, no deletion timeline after an account closes, and no shorter retention for AI interaction logs. The security section describes measures only as organizational, technical and administrative, and the policy never commits to notifying users of a breach.

highlights.title: Rights are offered, but conditioned on where you live
highlights.text: Access, correction, deletion and portability are all listed, each prefaced by "depending on your location" or "where applicable." The marketing opt-out is the one unconditional control, exercised through the unsubscribe link in each email. The policy does confirm it does not sell personal information or share it for interest-based advertising.

name: Domo
summary: Domo's privacy notice and service agreement cover individual rights, a 30-day post-termination export window and named transfer safeguards, but the service agreement grants Domo a sublicensable licence over customer data that survives termination, and the documents are silent on model training, children's protections and any named security certification.

highlights.title: Data licence reaches beyond service delivery
highlights.text: Customers keep ownership of Subscriber Data, but the agreement grants Domo a worldwide, royalty-free licence to sublicense, publish and distribute that data, and that licence is listed among the clauses that survive termination.

highlights.title: Export window is named, retention period is not
highlights.text: On written request before termination, the platform stays accessible for 30 days solely to download or export Subscriber Data, after which Domo has no obligation to retain it. For personal information held as a controller, retention runs "for as long as we have an ongoing legitimate need," with no stated period.

highlights.title: Rights are offered subject to law
highlights.text: Access, correction, erasure, portability and objection are listed with a privacy request form and a toll-free number, but the notice states some or all of these rights may not apply or may be subject to limitations depending on applicable law.

highlights.title: Silent on model training and children
highlights.text: The only training statement is a narrow commitment not to use Google Workspace APIs to train generalised AI or ML models. Neither document addresses whether customer data or inputs train Domo's own models, and neither sets an age gate or children's protections.

highlights.title: No retention period

highlights.title: Ads partners and no Do Not Track

highlights.title: Rights listed, routed through email

name: Pendo
summary: Pendo's policy is clear about who it shares data with and offers a named opt-out from ad-related sharing, but its strongest rights, transfer and legal-basis language sits in region-specific notices, it names no retention period, and its terms claim a perpetual sublicensable licence over anything users submit.

highlights.title: Perpetual licence over submissions
highlights.text: The terms of use take "a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free right and license (with right to sublicense)" over any content or feedback a user submits, including the right to make derivative works and exploit it for any purpose, and state that such content will not be treated confidentially.

highlights.title: No retention period
highlights.text: Pendo says it retains personal information "to fulfill the purposes for which we collected it" and lists factors it weighs, but names no number of days, months or years and gives no deletion timeline after an account closes.

highlights.title: Rights depend on where you live
highlights.text: Access, correction and deletion are set out in the California notice, and portability appears only in the notice to European users, so the global default text offers nothing more than reviewing account information in Settings.

highlights.title: AI use disclosed, with a hedge
highlights.text: Analytics and service improvement "may be supported by machine learning, otherwise known as artificially intelligent, functionality", which Pendo says it develops only after de-identifying, aggregating and/or anonymizing information, "although sometimes it may appear that such functionality was developed in a way that is specific to you".

summary: Cognition trains on customer data by default and offers an opt-out only to paying subscribers, with zero-retention available solely after that opt-out is exercised.

highlights.title: Training opt-out is paywalled
highlights.text: Customer Data may be used for model training and to improve the Services, and the opt-out is available only to subscribers on a paid Service Tier. On the Teams tier only an administrator can exercise it, so individual users cannot opt out for themselves.

highlights.title: Zero retention is conditional, not default
highlights.text: Zero Data Retention is defined as data never saved to disk and deleted once the Output is generated, but it switches on only after a paid-tier opt-out. The default retention rule is to keep information "as needed" with no stated number of days, and no deletion timeline follows account closure.

highlights.title: No named security controls or certification
highlights.text: Security is described only as "commercially reasonable technical, administrative, and organizational measures." No encryption standard, access-control model, or audit certification is named, and breach notice is promised only "as necessary to comply with applicable privacy laws.

highlights.title: Ownership granted, broad licence retained
highlights.text: Customers own their data and Outputs are assigned to them, yet the same terms take a worldwide, sublicensable, transferable licence over Customer Data. The stated age gate also conflicts: the privacy policy says 18 while the terms say 13.

name: Tabnine
summary: Tabnine's terms state that code written while using the service is used only to improve that same user's service and not to improve the service for other users, while the privacy policy names no retention period and places most of its concrete data rights inside sections that apply only to EU or California residents.

highlights.title: Your code stays yours
highlights.text: The terms state that Tabnine gains no rights in code you develop while using the service, and that such code is used only to improve the service provided specifically and solely to you, not to improve the service for other Tabnine users. The code-trained "Tailor Made" engine is provided only when you explicitly ask for it, and the code you share for it is not stored afterwards.

highlights.title: Rights depend on where you live
highlights.text: The globally applicable text offers only a request to access or modify your information by emailing support. Erasure, portability, rectification and objection are listed under rights that apply "in some jurisdictions, in particular" the EU and EEA, and the no-sale statement sits in the section written for California residents.

highlights.title: No retention period, no breach notice
highlights.text: Retention is described only as not longer than necessary for the service and for reasonable business and lawful needs, with no number given. Security is described as industry standard measures, and the policy commits to minimising harm after a breach rather than to notifying affected users within any timeframe.

name: Talkie
summary: Talkie discloses its data categories and purposes in detail and names a working ad opt-out, but it takes a perpetual sublicensable licence over user content, names no retention period, and names no safeguard for sending data abroad.

highlights.title: Content licence is perpetual and sublicensable
highlights.text: Uploading content grants Talkie and its affiliates a "transferable, sublicensable, perpetual, irrevocable license" to copy, modify, distribute and use that content for operating the service and for promotion, advertising or marketing. Users keep ownership of what they generate, but the grant does not expire when they leave.

highlights.title: No retention period, and no safeguard named for US transfers
highlights.text: Data is kept "for only as long as necessary" with no number attached. highlights.title: Ad sharing is disclosed with a real opt-out

highlights.title: Security controls and a privacy contact are named; breach timing is not
highlights.text: Stored data sits behind "firewalls, role-based access controls, and passwords" with encryption in transit, and a Data Protection Officer is reachable at a stated address and email. Breach notice is promised only "as soon as we spot the issue," with no deadline.

name: Forethought
summary: Forethought publishes a detailed rights section and a flat statement that it does not rent or sell personal information, but it says nothing about whether customer content trains its machine-learning models, names no retention period, and expressly reserves the right to change the policy without prior notice.

highlights.title: No training disclosure
highlights.text: The policy and SaaS agreement never address whether customer content is used to train Forethought's machine-learning models. The agreement instructs Forethought to use customer content to "provide, secure and improve" its products, with no opt-out named either way.

highlights.title: Retention left open-ended
highlights.text: Personal information is kept "for as long as is necessary for the purposes it was collected," and the policy adds that "actual retention periods can vary significantly." No number, no deletion timeline after an account closes, and no shorter window for AI conversation logs.

highlights.title: Changes without notice
highlights.text: Forethought "reserves the right to update or modify this Policy at any time and from time to time without prior notice." The page carries a Last Updated date but no version history, and material-change notice is only a "reasonable efforts" promise.

highlights.title: Transfer safeguard is Europe-only
highlights.text: The named safeguard, European Commission standard contractual clauses, is offered for transfers out of the EEA, UK and Switzerland. Users outside Europe get no equivalent named mechanism, and the site does not honour Do Not Track signals.

name: Qdrant
summary: Qdrant's privacy policy is a GDPR-style disclosure that spells out data subject rights, named transfer safeguards and a commitment not to use customer data for its own business purposes, while leaving breach notification, policy versioning and a government-access standard unaddressed.

highlights.title: Customer data is walled off from Qdrant's own use
highlights.text: The policy commits that Qdrant will not use data, information or material uploaded to the Cloud Service for its own business purposes, with carve-outs limited to supporting the customer's use, creating anonymized aggregated data, and cases the customer permits in writing. Model training is never mentioned anywhere in the policy.

highlights.title: Data subject rights are specific and article-cited
highlights.text: Access, correction, restriction, deletion, portability and objection are each tied to the GDPR article that grants them, portability specifies a structured, common and machine-readable format, access is free of charge, and direct-marketing objection routes to privacy@qdrant.com. A named external data protection officer at heyData GmbH is published with a postal address and email.

highlights.title: Retention is event-triggered rather than calendar-bound
highlights.text: Cloud Service personal data is kept as long as required and deleted upon termination or expiry of the customer agreement at the latest, subject to statutory retention. IP addresses in service log files are capped at 90 days, but the policy states the log files continue to be stored in anonymized form after the IP address is removed, with no end date.

highlights.title: Security, breach handling and policy change notice are thin
highlights.text: Encryption in transit is named as SSL, but everything beyond that is described only as appropriate technical and organizational measures, with no at-rest encryption, access control or certification named. The policy sets out no breach-notification commitment or timeframe, carries no version number or effective date, and promises only that a current version is always available.

name: Dust
summary: Dust's platform privacy policy is a clear GDPR-style disclosure with named data categories, named transfer safeguards, a named Data Protection Officer and a 16-plus age gate, but it is quiet on security specifics, breach notice and what happens to data after an account ends.

highlights.title: No-training commitment is limited to the model vendors
highlights.text: The policy says the foundational model providers it names, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Google and Fireworks, are prohibited from using customer and personal data for model training and apply a Zero Data Retention policy. It makes no equivalent statement about Dust's own use of platform data, and it names no opt-out or opt-in control a user could exercise.

highlights.title: Retention runs for years and the policy stops there
highlights.text: Personal data is kept for the agreement duration with customers and then archived for five years, with marketing data kept three years from last contact. The policy names no shorter retention for AI logs or prompts, and it never says how long deletion takes once an account or contract ends.

highlights.title: Security is described in adjectives, with no breach notice
highlights.text: The policy promises industry-standard physical, procedural and electronic measures and an encrypted database, but it names no encryption standard or access-control framework. There is no breach notification commitment anywhere in the text, and no named certification such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001.

highlights.title: Rights and transfers are concretely documented
highlights.text: The policy enumerates access, deletion, correction, restriction, portability, objection and consent withdrawal, routes them to privacy@dust.tt and a Data Protection Officer at dpo@dust.tt, and names Standard Contractual Clauses and European Commission adequacy decisions as the safeguards for transfers to the United States.

highlights.title: No retention period for Glean's own data

highlights.title: Gaps in security and sharing disclosure
highlights.text: Safeguards are described only as physical, administrative and technical, with no encryption, access-control or certification named. There is no breach-notification commitment, no sub-processor list or DPA reference, and the US-default California rights list omits data portability.

summary: Moveworks publishes a conventional business privacy policy with clear sharing categories, named international transfer safeguards and a firm no-sale promise, but it is silent on whether customer conversations train models, names no retention period, and gives no breach notification commitment.

name: DeepScribe
summary: DeepScribe's terms grant it a licence to run customer clinical recordings through machine learning with no opt-out offered, and let it keep and market de-identified data derived from those recordings after the contract ends, while the strongest privacy commitments sit in the HIPAA business associate agreement rather than the policy itself.

highlights.title: Training licence with no opt-out
highlights.text: Customers grant a worldwide, royalty-free licence to use and create derivative works from clinical recordings using machine learning and artificial intelligence, for improving DeepScribe's products as well as providing the service. The policy describes no way to decline.

highlights.title: De-identified data kept after the contract ends
highlights.text: DeepScribe may create de-identified data from customer recordings and, during and after the term, retain, share and use it for any legal purpose including marketing. That data is carved out of the protections that apply to customer data.

highlights.title: Retention and deletion left to DeepScribe's discretion
highlights.text: Personal data is kept "as long as it remains necessary" with no stated period, and if a customer stops using the service DeepScribe may retain or destroy everything at its own discretion. Returning or destroying health information on termination applies only "if feasible as determined by" DeepScribe.

highlights.title: Security named only in adjectives
highlights.text: The policy promises "reasonable steps" against loss and unauthorised access without naming encryption, access controls or any specific safeguard, and names no security certification or dedicated privacy contact. The one concrete number is a ten business day breach notification deadline in the business associate agreement.

highlights.title: Ask your boss, not 15Five

highlights.title: No clock on retention

highlights.title: Named audit, unnamed safeguards

name: Kling AI
summary: Kling AI's terms let the company train its models on the images, videos and prompts users upload, take a broad licence over both inputs and outputs, and state plainly that browser opt-out signals are ignored.

highlights.title: Your uploads train the models
highlights.text: The terms list creating, testing, improving and training the AI models used by Kling AI among the purposes for which uploaded content and inputs may be processed. Users who want this to stop must email support to revoke the authorisation; there is no setting or toggle, and a separate clause asks users not to claim rights over the company's use or development of that content.

highlights.title: A broad licence over inputs and outputs
highlights.text: Kling AI takes a non-exclusive, royalty-free licence to host, store, transfer, publicly display, reproduce, create derivative works from and distribute both the input provided and the output generated, in any media format and through any media channel. A further clause allows licensing that content to third parties for promotion and product research.

highlights.title: Opt-out signals are ignored
highlights.text: The policy states that Kling AI does not monitor, recognise or honour any opt-out or Do Not Track mechanism, including browser Do Not Track settings. The commitment not to sell personal data appears only in the California-specific section, not in the version that applies to most users.

highlights.title: No retention period and thin security detail
highlights.text: Data is kept "for as long as necessary" with no number attached, and the company reserves the right to delete data without notice. Security is described as "using encryption techniques" without naming a protocol or standard, and the unconditional data protection officer contact appears only in the Brazil and Singapore sections.

highlights.title: Never sells personal information

highlights.title: Thin on transfers and account closure
highlights.text: International transfers are covered only by a promise to comply with applicable law with no specific safeguard named, there is no stated deletion timeline after an account closes, and security controls are described as industry standard rather than itemised.

highlights.title: Retention has no clock

highlights.title: Security is described by adjective
highlights.text: Supio commits to "reasonable and appropriate precautions" without naming encryption, access controls or any certification, and the policy contains no breach notification commitment.

highlights.title: Security and breach handling are thin

name: Fathom
summary: Fathom records and transcribes meetings, trains its own AI models on de-identified meeting content unless you switch it off in account settings, and refuses to let outside AI vendors train on your data, but it stores personal information only "for as long as necessary" with no stated period and reserves the right to sell personal information in states whose law defines a sale broadly.

highlights.title: Training opt-out lives in your settings
highlights.text: De-identified data from meeting content trains Fathom's in-house AI models based on how you configure your account, and the policy points to a specific opt-out switch in account settings. It also states that third parties such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are not authorised to train on your data.

highlights.title: No retention period for meeting data
highlights.text: Personal information is kept "for as long as necessary" with no number attached. The only concrete clock is on exit: after an account deletion request Fathom says it will use commercially reasonable efforts to delete recordings within 30 days, and backup copies may persist for up to 30 days.

highlights.title: Sale of personal information is reserved
highlights.text: Depending on how a state's privacy law defines a "sale," Fathom may sell personal information to third parties, and opting out requires contacting the company. Meeting content and attendee information are carved out of this, and advertisers receive device information only.

highlights.title: Core rights are routed through regional law
highlights.text: Account deletion is self-service and the Global Privacy Control is honoured for everyone, but access, portability and correction appear as rights residents of the EEA, UK or particular US states "may have" rather than as commitments to all users.

highlights.title: Biometric data has a hard stop
highlights.text: Facial geometry and voiceprint processing requires consent and the data is deleted when no longer needed or once two years have passed since your last interaction with Zoom, whichever comes first.

highlights.title: Retention has no number
highlights.text: Personal data is kept "for as long as required to engage in the uses described" in the statement, with criteria listed but no stated period, no deletion timeline after account closure, and no shorter clock for AI logs.

highlights.title: Core rights are state-law gated
highlights.text: Access, deletion, correction and portability are framed as rights residents "may have" under some U.S. state laws, are described as not absolute, and may not be afforded to residents of all states.

name: Darktrace
summary: Darktrace publishes a detailed enterprise privacy notice with a named Data Protection Officer and broad GDPR-style rights, but its AI recruitment disclosures admit training data cannot be withdrawn and the notice sets no retention periods, no breach-notification commitment, and no children's or automated-decision protections.

highlights.title: Training data is irreversible
highlights.text: Personal data processed through the Paradox recruitment platform trains its LLMs, and the notice states that because model training is not reversible, data already used cannot be withdrawn or removed from trained models. Candidates who decline can request an alternative non-AI method, but anyone who uses the Olivia chat tool cannot opt out of the AI processing.

highlights.title: No retention period is named
highlights.text: Data is kept for as long as reasonably necessary, with longer retention where litigation is anticipated. Actual retention schedules are not published and must be requested from the Data Protection Officer.

highlights.title: Rights are strong, security detail is thin
highlights.text: Access, correction, erasure, restriction, objection and opt-out are all offered through a named privacy address, and an internal Data Protection Officer is named with full contact details. highlights.title: Website analytics sit outside the no-sale claim
highlights.text: Darktrace does not sell data captured through its products or services, yet concedes that Google Analytics on its public website may count as exchanging data for valuable consideration under CCPA, leaving a browser add-on as the opt-out.

name: Drata
summary: Drata commits in its terms that it does not use customer data to train or fine-tune AI models and does not permit its inference providers to do so, gates AI features behind an administrator opt-in, and names a 48-hour security incident notification window, while its retention, security-control and sensitive-data language stays general.

highlights.title: No model training
highlights.text: The terms state that Drata does not use Customer Data to train or fine-tune artificial intelligence or machine learning models, and that third-party inference providers are not permitted to do so either. Data sent to AI features is described as processed on a transient basis and not retained by the inference provider after a response is generated.

highlights.title: AI is off until an admin turns it on
highlights.text: AI features are available only if a customer enables them through administrative settings in the service, and can be disabled again at any time. Free-trial data carries an explicit warning that it is permanently lost unless the customer buys a subscription or exports it before the trial ends.

highlights.title: Retention stated without a number
highlights.text: The privacy notice says personal data is generally retained as long as necessary for the purposes it was collected for, naming no retention period. Customer data stays exportable for thirty days after termination, after which deletion follows a separate policy kept in the Trust Center rather than in the published terms.

highlights.title: Security described in general terms
highlights.text: The notice commits to appropriate security procedures and technical and organizational measures without naming specific controls such as encryption standards or access models. Against that, a security incident triggers notice to the customer within forty-eight hours, and a data protection officer is named with a postal contact.

name: Veriff
summary: Veriff's privacy notice is detailed about how its verification engine and machine learning work, but it routes most end-user rights requests to the customer who commissioned the verification, gives no general retention period, and puts its firmest biometric deletion deadline only in a state-specific section.

highlights.title: Rights run through the customer
highlights.text: Where Veriff processed the data to deliver a verification, the notice says a request to know, delete, correct or port must be submitted to the customer who is the data controller rather than to Veriff, and the rights list itself opens with "depending on where you reside, you may have the right".

highlights.title: No general retention period
highlights.text: Data is kept "for as long as necessary to carry out the purposes for which we originally collected it", with end-user retention set by each customer agreement. No number is given, and the only concrete figures are a one-day demo window and state-specific biometric deadlines.

highlights.title: Training on real session data
highlights.text: Algorithms are built, trained and tested on training sets consisting of real data or anonymized data for internal service improvement, done on a contractual mandate from the customer. No opt-out mechanism is offered to the person being verified.

highlights.title: Named engine and human review
highlights.text: The notice describes a verification engine trained with machine learning, labels each process as automated, semi-automated or human, and states a right to request human intervention or object to a fully automated decision.
